node.date_label: 1835 De la démocratie en Amérique — first part · 1840 De la démocratie en Amérique — second part · 1856 L’Ancien Régime et la Révolution
node.description: Alexis de Tocqueville investigated democratic society and the historical conditions of revolutionary change while also writing and acting as a political thinker. De la démocratie en Amérique appeared in two parts; L’Ancien Régime et la Révolution returned to prerevolutionary France. In its preface he explains his use of cahiers, provincial records and administrative archives, asking how practices and social relations survived apparent rupture. His study is an earlier historical inquiry into power and society, not membership in a twentieth-century historiographical school.
node.representative_figures_and_works: De la démocratie en Amérique — first part (1835); De la démocratie en Amérique — second part (1840); L’Ancien Régime et la Révolution (1856).
node.scope_note: Read only the 1856 Avant-propos at 5–12; Democracy in America and the remaining Old Regime text remain unread. Connections describe an earlier historical programme, not membership in twentieth-century schools. The joint penitentiary report with Gustave de Beaumont is not treated as a sole-authored work; the Académie’s unverified 1832 date is not adopted. The exact frozen first-author key P:tocqueville|alexis has 104 dated dissertation appearances; this retains the reviewed provisional screening qualification and does not verify every fragment or imply influence. Complete monographs remain unread except the specified selected passages. Existing identities, collective relationships, roster prose and source qualifications remain intact. proposed_edges.relationship: Investigates administrative continuity across revolutionary rupture
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The 1856 Avant-propos at 5–12 asks how habits and institutions from the monarchy persisted after 1789. This is an earlier historical inquiry into political change, not membership in a modern school.

proposed_edges.relationship: Uses administrative archives to investigate relations among classes and everyday governance
proposed_edges.evidence_note: At 7–10, Tocqueville describes moving beyond celebrated writers and public figures toward institutional practices, relations among classes and provincial administrative archives. This is his research programme; it does not make every archival voice representative.
